objectives: Hear and identify /p/ in familiar word positions.
Discriminate /p/ from previously taught consonants m, s and t.
Prepare for decoding and spelling new CVC words containing p.
concepts: A new grapheme should be explicitly connected to its phoneme before independent use.
Phoneme position matters: /p/ can occur at the beginning or end of a familiar CVC word.
New phonics content should build on secure prior correspondences.

definitions.definition: A smallest unit of sound that can change word meaning.
A letter or group of letters used to represent a sound in writing.

commonMistakes: Selecting p without saying the sound.
Using p in a word position without listening to the whole word.
keyTakeaways: Check the sound position in a word.
revisionPoints: p represents /p/ in this taught set.

conceptual: Compare /p/ with m, s and t.
application: Select or write p after hearing /p/.
higherOrderThinking: Explain why explicit sound-letter mapping supports later decoding.

mistakeBasedRevision: If p is confused with another consonant, return to isolated sound discrimination before word reading.
weakTopicRevision: Use short spoken-word sorting for initial and final /p/, then repeat grapheme selection.

activities.name: Sound hunt
steps: Show whether /p/ is at the beginning or end.

activities.name: Grapheme match
steps: Mix p with m, s and t and repeat.

outcomes: Learner identifies /p/ in at least 8 of 10 familiar spoken words.
Learner selects the grapheme p for /p/ with at least 90% accuracy.
Learner distinguishes /p/ from taught m, s and t sounds.

questions.question: Which sound does the letter p usually represent in these lessons?
Which word has /p/ as its final sound?
Which pair begins with the same /p/ sound?
Which word begins with a different sound from the others?
What should you do when learning a new letter-sound?
options: Hear the sound, say it, identify it and connect it to the letter
Guess the word from a picture

questions.question: Which letter should you write after hearing /p/?
Why is it important to teach /p/ before using it in new spelling work?
options: The learner needs the sound-letter relationship as a prerequisite
It removes the need for blending

questions.question: Which word ends with /p/ and has short /a/ in the middle?
Which activity best teaches /p/ discrimination?
options: Sort spoken words by whether they begin or end with /p/

questions.question: If a learner writes 'b' after hearing /p/, what needs practice?
options: The /p/ sound and its grapheme connection

questions.question: What shows that the /p/ sound is becoming secure?
options: The learner identifies /p/, selects p and uses it accurately in familiar words
The learner guesses words from pictures
The learner avoids words with p
The learner only names the alphabet
